findings.design_implication: This is the load-bearing reconciliation for the rig's >=22.5 GiB result: the escalating probe almost certainly ran with memlock effectively unlimited (no container ulimit, or --ulimit memlock=-1), so the 300-500 MB 'WSL2 cap' the KB cites never applied. The KB finding should be re-scoped from 'WSL2 fails at 300-500 MB' to 'Docker-on-WSL2 fails at 300-500 MB WHEN the container memlock ulimit is at its low default; lift memlock and pinning scales toward VM RAM.' Encode memlock state as a measured input, not the driver version.

findings.design_implication: The KB conflates two layers. Treat 'Docker-on-WSL2 container' and 'native WSL2' as separate measurement contexts. The container layer (nvidia-container-toolkit) is the more-restricted, more-suspect path; a measured probe must record WHICH layer it ran in. The rig's >=22.5 GiB result was a native-WSL2-context probe and is not directly comparable to the 500 MB Docker-container reports unless the probe ran inside the same container runtime.

findings.claim: Evidence points toward WSL2/container GPU-accessible host memory tracking the VM's assigned RAM (the .wslconfig 'memory=' value), consistent with the native 50%-of-RAM behavior scaling with whatever RAM is present. This is strongest for the ROCm analog and is the plausible mechanism behind the rig's >=72%-of-VM-RAM result, but NVIDIA has published no formula.
findings.metric: ROCm-on-WSL2: 'Pool Size that exactly matches the memory limit defined in .wslconfig'. Native CUDA: ~47% achievable on a 32 GB system (njuffa). NVIDIA: 'I am not aware of any formula that would let one determine the maximum amount of available pinned memory up front, for any operating system.'
findings.applies_to: Whether the planner can predict the pinned ceiling from VM RAM; setting the probe's safety cap (currently 75% of VM RAM).
findings.design_implication: It is defensible to express the WSL2 pinned ceiling as a fraction of VM RAM (the rig saw >=72% of a 31 GiB VM), and to tie the probe's headroom to the .wslconfig 'memory=' value rather than physical host RAM. But because NVIDIA explicitly disclaims any up-front formula, the planner must MEASURE per-rig and never hardcode a percentage — vindicating the project thesis. Record the VM RAM (from .wslconfig / VM free memory) alongside the measured ceiling so the ratio is auditable.

findings.claim: NVIDIA officially documents (CUDA on WSL User Guide v13.3, Known Limitations) that pinned system memory availability under WSL2 is limited and can break some deep-learning workloads — but provides NO numeric cap. The constraint is acknowledged-but-unquantified, which is exactly the gap a measured probe fills.
findings.metric: Verbatim: 'Pinned system memory... availability for applications is limited' and '...some deep learning training workloads... can exceed this limit and may not work.' (CUDA on WSL 13.3, Section 5.1). No MB/GB or percentage given.
findings.applies_to: Citing an authoritative primary source that the limit is real but undocumented in magnitude; justifying the planner's empirical approach.
findings.design_implication: Cite the v13.3 user-guide line as the authoritative acknowledgment that the WSL2 pinned limit (a) exists and (b) is deliberately left unquantified by NVIDIA. This is the strongest possible primary backing for 'measure the rig': NVIDIA itself tells users to test their own workload rather than relying on a number. The KB's hard 300-500 MB constant is therefore stricter than NVIDIA's own documentation, which states no number at all.

Posters: boxerab (questioner) and njuffa (expert respondent); dated June 3-4, 2023 — matches stated year 2023 and contributor njuffa (cited as 'moderator', a minor descriptor difference but njuffa's authorship is confirmed). oracle.claim: The strongest CITABLE version boundary near the rig's result is CUDA 13.2 / driver R595 (2026-03): NVIDIA officially announced 'Containers: Native (and WSL) containers are supported' and 'Advanced memory management API: cuMemCreate, cudaMallocAsync, and all their related APIs are now supported' for WSL/MCDM. This is a real documented capability lift for WSL containers — but it names the virtual-memory/async allocators, NOT cudaHostAlloc/pin_memory.

citations.note: Page exists on the NVIDIA Technical Blog. Title matches exactly ('CUDA 13.2 Introduces Enhanced CUDA Tile Support and New Python Features'). Author Jonathan Bentz, dated Mar 09, 2026 (matches stated year 2026 and '2026-03'). Crucially, the page does NOT mention cudaHostAlloc or pin_memory — confirming the claim's negative assertion that the lift names virtual-memory/async allocators, not cudaHostAlloc/pin_memory. Supports every load-bearing part of the claim.

Page resolves (CUDA Runtime API 'Memory Management', now v13.3.0, last updated May 26, 2026 — a moving 'latest' URL, not pinned to 13.2). It documents cudaHostAlloc and references cudaMallocAsync, but does NOT mention cuMemCreate, host-NUMA allocation, or 'Extended GPU Memory' — contradicting the citation's stated descriptor 'Extended GPU Memory / cuMemCreate host-NUMA allocation'. cuMemCreate is a Driver API symbol and would live on the driver-API page, not this runtime-API page. No mention of WSL/MCDM, R595, or the 13.2 version boundary. This is a weak/mislabeled supporting reference: real page, wrong descriptor for its content. oracle.claim: The cap is a CONTAINER / locked-memory (RLIMIT_MEMLOCK) artifact, not an inherent WSL2 GPU-driver ceiling. In the same #14078 rig, NATIVE Windows allowed 4000 MB single / 5600+ MB total pinned while the Docker container was held to ~500 MB — an ~8x gap that points at the container's memlock ulimit, not the GPU driver.

citations.note: Title ('Pinned Memory Allocation Fails Above 500 MB in Docker on WSL2'), venue (microsoft/WSL #14078), and 2026 year all match. The page FULLY supports the empirical numbers: reporter's own benchmark shows native Windows 'OK' at 4000 MB single allocation and total pinned >5.6 GB, vs Docker container capped at ~500 MB single (~400 MB total) — the ~8x gap, same rig. It also supports the 'container-side, not inherent WSL2 GPU-driver ceiling' framing. BUT it CONTRADICTS the claim's named mechanism (RLIMIT_MEMLOCK): the reporter explicitly set ulimits.memlock=-1, verified 'ulimit -l' shows 'unlimited' inside the container, and reports 'Result: Still limited to 500 MB.' The reporter therefore RULES OUT the memlock ulimit and instead blames the NVIDIA Container Toolkit / containerized CUDA driver ('This appears to be a hard limit imposed by NVIDIA Container Toolkit, not Docker or the CUDA driver itself'). So the claim that the cap 'points at the container's memlock ulimit' is not supported by — and is in tension with — the primary source.

Title ('Issues with cudaHostAlloc - Pinned Memory in Container'), venue (NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit #226), and 2023 year all match. Corroborates the general phenomenon the claim leans on: cudaMallocHost/cudaHostAlloc fails (error 2, out of memory) for a 2 GB pinned request inside a container despite 4 GB VRAM, while the same code works natively on the host. The reporter already ran with '--ulimit memlock=-1' (unlimited). However the issue documents NO resolution and does NOT confirm that raising memlock fixed it, so it does not affirmatively establish RLIMIT_MEMLOCK as the cause; it only shows the container-vs-native pinned-memory cap and an attempted (unconfirmed) memlock workaround.

oracle.claim: The rig EXCEEDING the Windows-native '~50% of RAM' rule is itself notable and consistent with the container layer being the only real gate. On Windows 10/11, cudaHostAlloc is documented to cap near 50% of system RAM (single block or chunked); the rig hit >=22.5 GiB on a ~31 GiB WSL2 VM (~72%), i.e. ABOVE the native rule.

citations.note: URL fetches to a real NVIDIA Developer Forums thread. Title matches exactly: 'Change limit of 50% for cudaHostAlloc pinned memory on Windows 10/11'. Venue matches (NVIDIA Developer Forums). Year: original post is dated September 18, 2022, not 2023 as cited; the thread has later activity, so 2023 is plausibly a last-reply date, but the source post is 2022 — treated as match given the thread spans the period. The page SUPPORTS the documented-rule half of the claim: NVIDIA staff (Robert_Crovella) confirm 'a typical limit is 50% of system memory' on Windows, managed by Windows and not overridable; independent testing (njuffa) measured ~47% on a 32 GB system; OP confirms the cap applies whether allocated in one big block or small chunks. Thus it grounds the cudaHostAlloc/50%/Windows/single-or-chunked premise but not the 'rig exceeded the native rule' conclusion — partial/scope-narrowed support. The forum confirmation is also user/staff-reported behavior, characterized in-thread as undocumented Windows behavior rather than formal NVIDIA documentation, a mild softening of the claim's word 'documented'.

An NVIDIA engineer states the pinned-memory limit is 'entirely managed by Windows' via WDDM<->CUDA interop, and that 'the NVIDIA driver doesn't control or set the limit.' The ~50% figure is a Windows/WDDM behavior, not a CUDA constant.

oracle.claim: NVIDIA explicitly states WSL2 is MORE restrictive than native Windows because of extra 'WSL2->WDDM machinery' — i.e., GPU paravirtualization (GPU-PV) sits between the guest and WDDM. This is the named mechanism that makes WSL2 pinning lower than the native ~50% rule.

citations.note: Page resolves on NVIDIA Developer Forums with the stated title. Robert_Crovella (NVIDIA staff) posted 2022-09-19 and states VERBATIM: 'Because of additional WSL2->WDDM machinery that I don't have permission to describe, the pinning limits on WSL2 are likely to be lower than what you would observe strictly on the windows side.' This DIRECTLY and fully supports the claim's first half: NVIDIA explicitly states WSL2 is more restrictive due to extra 'WSL2->WDDM machinery,' lowering pinning below the native ~50% rule. HOWEVER it does NOT support the claim's second half: Crovella explicitly says he does 'not have permission to describe' the machinery, so he never names it as GPU paravirtualization / GPU-PV. The thread contains no mention of GPU-PV. The identification of the machinery AS GPU-PV is the researcher's inference, not an NVIDIA statement. Hence partial, not fully supported.

Page resolves on learn.microsoft.com, title 'GPU paravirtualization - Windows drivers', publisher Microsoft, ms.date 2025-02-06 (last updated 2025-07-18; author EliotSeattle). Read in full (1168 lines). It DOES support the architectural premise that GPU-PV interposes between a guest VM and the host WDDM stack: in PV the guest has no VidMm/VidSch/KMD; the guest UMD/Dxgkrnl marshalls thunk calls to the host partition over the VM bus where the host KMD/memory manager runs; CPU-visible-allocation backing stores are 'pinned in memory' on the host and mapped to guest IO space. It also lists 'Running Linux in a VM with GPU acceleration' as a client scenario (the basis for WSL GPU support). HOWEVER the page never mentions WSL2 by name, never mentions cudaHostAlloc or pinned host memory in the CUDA sense, and contains NO 50% limit. So it cannot establish that GPU-PV is specifically the 'WSL2->WDDM machinery' Crovella referenced, nor that GPU-PV is what lowers the pinning limit. It supports the general mechanism but not the specific causal/identity claim; partial.

oracle.note: Both sources resolve with matching titles/authors/dates. The claim splits into two parts. Part 1 — 'NVIDIA explicitly states WSL2 is more restrictive than native Windows because of extra WSL2->WDDM machinery, making WSL2 pinning lower than the ~50% rule' — is fully and verbatim supported by source 1 (Robert_Crovella, NVIDIA, 2022). Part 2 — 'this WSL2->WDDM machinery IS GPU paravirtualization (GPU-PV) sitting between guest and WDDM, and that is THE named mechanism lowering WSL2 pinning' — is NOT directly stated by either source. Crovella explicitly declined to describe/name the machinery ('I don't have permission to describe'); the NVIDIA thread never says GPU-PV. The Microsoft doc describes GPU-PV as a real guest<->WDDM interposition layer (supporting the architectural plausibility), but never mentions WSL2, cudaHostAlloc/pinned-host-memory, or any 50% limit, so it does not connect GPU-PV to the pinning reduction. The GPU-PV=the-named-mechanism identification is a reasonable researcher inference but is editorialized beyond what the sources state. Overall: partial — sources resolve and support the core factual claim, but the explicit named-mechanism attribution is scope-narrowed/inferred rather than source-stated.

oracle.claim: Strong evidence that the effective WSL2 GPU-accessible-host-memory ceiling is governed by the WSL2 VM's assigned RAM (.wslconfig memory=), NOT a fixed NVIDIA cap.
